title: Verifying Coordination in Parallel Coding Agents: NP-Bench and a Scheduling Planner
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Verifying Coordination in Parallel Coding Agents: NP-Bench and a Scheduling Planner
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A team of coding agents can look fine agent by agent yet fail as a team: each passes its own tests while the merged result is broken, and single-agent evaluation never catches it. As teams run several LLM coding agents in parallel on one codebase, the agents collide: two rewrite the same function, one codes against a contract a teammate just changed, and integration fails after the work is done. Most coordination tools react (watch for a conflict, then warn), but at agent speed the warning arrives after the wasted edit. We recast the problem as scheduling: take each work item's declared scope, partition the work into disjoint scopes, and order merges along the producer->consumer graph, all up front. We build this planner into Nerveplane and evaluate it with NP-Bench, an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark (no coordination; reactive detection; proactive planning) that verifies integration off a real git merge, both in a deterministic simulation and with live agents. The planner lifts clean-integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and cuts merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with a gap that grows in the number of agents. On a live breaking contract change it rescues an outcome both baselines miss on every seed: the clean-integration rate rises from 0 (no coordination and reactive detection) to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small one, while agents respect assigned scopes (0/5 leakage). A cross-session memory drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on strong and weak models alike. We also report a negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales; its value is cost and capacity, not attention. Across two capability tiers and two vendors, the benefit did not shrink as models got stronger, because it comes from how work is allocated, not model reasoning.

report.summary: A new planner schedules parallel coding agents into disjoint scopes and merge order, lifting clean git integration from 1/9 to 9/9 and eliminating merge conflicts.
report.background: Multi-agent coding is moving from demos to real codebases, where several LLM agents edit the same repository in parallel. Single-agent evaluation misses team-level failures: each agent passes its own tests while the merged result breaks. Agents collide by rewriting the same function, coding against a contract a teammate just changed, or failing integration after work is done. Most coordination tools are reactive: they detect a conflict and warn, but at agent speed the warning arrives after the wasted edit. This paper recasts coordination as scheduling. Using each work item's declared scope, Nerveplane partitions work into disjoint scopes and orders merges along the producer-to-consumer graph up front. NP-Bench is an environment-grounded three-arm benchmark, run in deterministic simulation and with live agents, verifying integration via real git merges.
key_points: Per-agent tests can look perfect while the team fails: parallel agents collide when they edit the same function, depend on changed contracts, or merge conflicting work. NP-Bench verifies full integration with a real git merge, not just individual agent tests.

Proactive planning beats both no coordination and reactive conflict detection. The scheduler lifts clean integration from 1/9 to 9/9 scenarios and cuts merge conflicts from 13 to 0, with the advantage growing as the number of agents increases.

On a live breaking contract change, the planner rescues an outcome both baselines miss on every seed. Clean-integration rate rises from 0 under no coordination and reactive detection to 1.0 on a frontier model and 0.6 on a small model, with 0/5 scope leakage.

A cross-session memory mechanism drops the repeated-mistake rate from 1.00 to 0.00 on both strong and weak models. This suggests memory and scope discipline matter independently of raw model reasoning.

A negative result: routing facts to agents does not rescue long-context accuracy at window-fitting scales. Its value is cost and capacity, not attention. The planner's benefit did not shrink across two capability tiers and two vendors.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts multi-agent orchestration from reactive conflict detection to up-front scheduling. Instead of watching for collisions, systems can declare work scopes, partition ownership, and order merges by dependency. That could make parallel coding agents viable on shared codebases and create demand for coordination benchmarks like NP-Bench. For developers, the lesson is that team-level verification and scope enforcement belong in the agent workflow, alongside tests and review. For regular users, agent-built features may arrive faster and with fewer broken merges, but the planner does not improve model reasoning or long-context attention. It allocates work better; it does not replace testing, contracts, or human oversight.
report.tools: Watch Nerveplane, the scheduling planner described in the paper, and NP-Bench for evaluating multi-agent coordination. Related tools include LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI for agent orchestration; git worktrees and merge queues for parallel branches; Graphite, Mergify, and CodeRabbit for merge and review automation; and SWE-bench for coding-agent evaluation.
